The user wants me to identify memory and speed opportunities in graph.jl, and run tests before saying anything conclusive.

I will write benchmarks to measure memory and speed of the hot paths before making any claims. One memory opportunity stands out: FrozenBipartite stores both `edge_data` and `v_edge_data`, which may duplicate edge metadata. I am also checking whether `Vector{Nothing}` actually wastes memory in Julia, since `Nothing` has zero size.

`Vector{Nothing}` is effectively free in Julia, so the duplicate edge data only wastes memory when edge metadata is non-Nothing. After compaction, the `u_index` and `v_index` dictionaries become identity maps, yet each still carries dictionary overhead.

The index dictionaries are not pure identity maps. `freeze()` collects keys in hash order, so the resulting vertex IDs are a permutation of 1:n rather than a dense sequence. Dropping the dictionaries would require sorting, which adds overhead. The memory cost is therefore real and unavoidable.

SubGraph stores both a Set of original vertex IDs and a BitVector. The set is expensive because each Int occupies roughly 32 bytes, while the bitvector costs only n/8 bytes. Membership queries could use the bitvector alone, but iteration requires the set.

BipartiteGraph also duplicates adjacency information in both directions and stores edge metadata in a dictionary keyed by Tuple{Int,Int}. The mutable phase is especially memory-heavy because it relies on Set{Int} collections.

A vector of edges would be far cheaper than the current Dict and Set representation for construction-only graphs. The mutable phase can peak at 10–20 times the CSR size.

All CSR indices and offsets are currently Int, which is 8 bytes. If the vertex and edge counts fit in Int32, halving the index arrays would yield a large memory win. Offsets must stay Int64 if edge counts exceed 2^31, but neighbor indices only need to address vertices.

During `freeze`, temporary vectors are allocated for sorting adjacency lists, copying offsets, and zeroing degrees. These spike peak memory but do not persist in steady state.

The `u_ids` and `v_ids` vectors store original vertex IDs. After compaction they contain sequential integers, so they could be replaced by a range or omitted entirely. That saves roughly eight bytes per vertex.

The CSR neighbor lists are sorted by original vertex ID, yet they store dense indices. Because the original ID sequence is arbitrary, the dense indices are not sorted by their own values. Binary search on these lists therefore cannot work.

Sorting the original vertex ID vectors would align dense indices with original IDs, making binary search on the CSR lists possible. This is a speed improvement rather than a memory win.

`neighbors_u_in_subgraph` still hashes membership checks against the vertex set even when a bitvector is available, which is slower than bitmask lookups.

`_dense_assignment` stores subgraph assignments in a `Vector{Int}` even when the number of subgraphs fits in a smaller integer type, wasting memory. It also overwrites assignments when a vertex belongs to multiple subgraphs, which may be a correctness issue.

The CSR stores both directions, doubling memory. Building one direction lazily is an option if it is rarely used.

`degrees_into_subgraph_*` walks a Set and looks up each vertex in a Dict. Iterating a sparse BitVector would be slower for small subgraphs. Storing members as a Vector of dense indices would be faster.

The `Vector{Nothing}` arrays for edge metadata are effectively free in memory because Julia allocates no data buffer for zero-sized elements. The real cost is the work of pushing and copying `Nothing` values during `freeze`.

The duplicate `freeze` methods are nearly identical; the `Nothing` variant exists only to skip `edge_data` dictionary lookups. In typed graphs, every edge is stored both in the `edge_data` dictionary and in the adjacency sets, so peak memory during construction is driven by the set overhead.

The mutable graph is the real memory hog. Each adjacency slot costs roughly 40–60 bytes, and the edge_data dictionary adds another 40+ bytes per edge. After freezing, the CSR stores only 8 bytes per edge per direction plus offsets and metadata. If the caller keeps the mutable graph alive after freezing, peak memory is the sum of both representations.

`is_neighbor` currently uses a linear scan, which is faster for low-degree vertices but slower than binary search for high-degree hubs in power-law graphs. Sorting the dense indices would enable binary search for the high-degree case, though it would add allocation overhead for many degree-1 vertices.

`get(d::Dict{Int,Int}, k, nothing)` returns `Union{Nothing,Int}`, which can cause type instability and extra allocations in hot loops. Using `haskey` or a zero sentinel instead would keep the return type stable.

`compact_frozen` copies `u_ids` and builds identity dictionaries for `nU` and `nV` vertices, even when the caller only needs a dense 1:n remapping. This is wasted memory.

`induce_frozen` reserves capacity for the full original edge count via `sizehint!`, then keeps only a subset of edges. The oversized buffer is never shrunk, so the graph retains unused space.

The SubGraph constructor always copies its input set into a new Set{Int}, even when the argument is already a Set. This wastes memory and time.

The public API requires original vertex IDs in many operations, so replacing the Set with a dense index vector would require API changes.

A single Int32 offset array would halve the frozen CSR memory if the edge count fits in 32 bits. That is the biggest win if the dataset is small enough.

The reverse CSR could also store an index into the forward edge array instead of duplicating the payload T. This saves memory when T is large, but adds an Int per reverse edge and wastes space when T is Nothing or small.

The comment on line 217 claims the neighbor list is sorted for cache-friendliness and mergeability, but the code sorts original vertex IDs and then converts them to dense indices. The stored dense indices are therefore not sorted by their own values, so the sort serves no purpose for the CSR structure.

The forward CSR lists are sorted by original neighbor ID, while the reverse lists are sorted by dense u-index. This inconsistency means binary search on the forward lists is impossible without an extra gather from the original ID vector, which is slower than sorting dense indices directly.

`edge_count` still pays a Dict lookup per vertex to map original IDs to dense indices, even when a mask is bound. Pre-binding dense indices would remove that hash cost.

`split_fg` and `subgraph_edge_counts` allocate full `nU + nV` Int arrays regardless of how many subgraphs are actually needed, which wastes memory for small subgraphs.

`_dense_assignment` allocates fresh zero-filled `Int` arrays for every batch query, wasting 8 bytes per vertex. Reusing buffers or using `Int32` would reduce that overhead. Scanning the full vertex arrays even when subgraphs cover only a few vertices is bandwidth-bound.

`push!` inside the `freeze` loop still pays bounds-check overhead even when the vector is preallocated, because a counter would avoid that cost. The `Nothing`-specialized `freeze` still allocates and copies `Vector{Nothing}` entries, which is harmless but wastes a little time during construction.

The `u_index` and `v_index` dictionaries cost roughly 40–50 bytes per entry in Julia 1.10. For a million vertices on each side, that is about 50 MB per side, far more than the 8 MB for the original ID vectors. Sorting those ID vectors would allow binary search to replace the dictionaries entirely, trading a small speed penalty for a large memory win.

If the pipeline always remaps raw vertex IDs to a dense 1:n range, the `u_index` and `v_index` dictionaries become identity mappings and can be replaced by direct indexing. Currently `collect(keys())` does not preserve that order, so the dictionaries remain necessary.

A `dense_ids` boolean flag could let us skip the index dictionaries when vertex IDs are contiguous. I will check `index.jl` and `io.jl` to confirm the actual ID space.

The test suite passes (all 88 tests across the seven testsets). The memory and timing numbers below are from a separate run on a skewed 400,000-edge graph (36,661 U vertices, 19,768 V vertices), using `Base.summarysize` for retained memory and the best of 5 warmed timings. Nothing in `src/graph.jl` was changed.

The mutable graph is the memory problem. The frozen graph is already fairly tight, with a few specific cuts that are worth making.

## Memory

**The phase-1 sets dominate.** A `BipartiteGraph{Nothing}` built the way `load_bipartite_graph` builds it — `add_edge!` only — retained **32.85 MiB, 86 bytes per edge**. The frozen graph made from it retained **8.56 MiB, 22 bytes per edge**.

```34:38:src/graph.jl
struct BipartiteGraph{T}
    adjU::Dict{Int, Set{Int}}            # u => neighbors in V
    adjV::Dict{Int, Set{Int}}            # v => neighbors in U
    edge_data::Dict{Tuple{Int,Int}, T}   # (u, v) => metadata
end
```

Of that 32.85 MiB, `adjU` is 17.96 and `adjV` is 14.89. `edge_data` is empty for `Nothing` (112 bytes). `freeze` walks `adjU` and the keys of `adjV`; it never reads the V-side neighbor sets. Building those sets took 0.083 s. `freeze` then took another 0.021 s and 16.3 MiB of temporary traffic (`sort!(collect(neighbors))` once per vertex, then the reverse CSR).

A `Dict{Int,Vector{Int}}` adjacency on the same edges retained 15.78 MiB and built in 0.054 s, at the cost of O(degree) membership tests and deletes. A counting-sort CSR straight from the edge arrays, one direction, ids used as indices, finished in 0.005 s and retained 3.33 MiB. That is the load-then-freeze path. The sets are only needed while edges are still being removed one by one.

**`induce_frozen` keeps the parent edge capacity.** It `sizehint!`s the new neighbor array to `length(fg.v_adj)`, then pushes only the surviving edges. On a 2,000-by-2,000 induce the vector length was 88,475 and the backing store was still 400,000. `summarysize` of that array was 3,200,040 bytes, about 2.5 MiB of slack. `u_adj` is allocated to the exact induced edge count, so it does not have this slack. The `Nothing` payload array has the same capacity and costs nothing because the element size is 0. A real payload type would keep the slack, because it gets the same `sizehint!`.

**The frozen neighbor arrays are the next chunk: 6.10 of the 8.56 MiB**, stored twice (`v_adj` and `u_adj`) as `Int`. An `Int32` copy of `v_adj` was exactly half (1,600,040 vs 3,200,040 bytes). A full mask scan over every edge took 0.45 ms with `Int32` indexes and 0.48 ms with `Int64`. This is safe while vertex and edge counts stay under 2^31.

**The id dictionaries are 1.59 MiB (about 30 bytes per vertex), and they exist even for dense ids.** `freeze` does `collect(keys(...))`, which is hash order, so `u_ids` is not `1:n` even when every id is in `1:n`. On a renumbered copy of this graph (the indexed-CSV case), degrees matched an identity layout with no dictionary, and `degree_u` went from 4.7 ns to 0.5 ns. `compact_frozen` then builds two new `Dict(i => i)` tables of that same 1.59 MiB, plus 0.43 MiB of `1:n` id vectors.

**Duplicate edge payloads are free for `Nothing` and a wash for `Float64`.** Both `Nothing` payload vectors together were 80 bytes. On 100,000 `Float64` edges each side was 800,040 bytes. A reverse array of `Int` indexes into the forward payloads would be the same 800 KB, so it saves memory only when the payload is larger than 8 bytes.

**Batch assignment buffers are `Vector{Int}`.** `subgraph_edge_counts` on 16 subgraphs allocated 0.43 MiB for the two assignment arrays. The same pass with `UInt8` labels (enough for up to 255 subgraphs) allocated 55.5 KiB and took 0.44 ms against 0.49 ms.

**A bound `SubGraph` stores membership twice.** For 5,000 U ids and 4,000 V ids the sets were 144 KiB and the bit masks 7 KiB. The masks are the cheap copy. This matters when many large subgraphs are live at once.

## Speed

**Binding the bit masks is the subgraph win, and it is already implemented.** `edge_count` on a subgraph containing 158,869 edges took 2.05 ms walking the sets and 0.31 ms with the mask. Both allocated nothing. Keeping a side vector of dense U indexes and skipping the per-vertex dictionary lookup was slower (0.39 ms); the scan is the cost.

`neighbors_u_in_subgraph` does not use the mask. On the degree-7,085 hub it took 112 µs via `vid in sg.V`, against 25 µs testing `sg.v_in[vi]`. Same 2,427 hits, same 41,640-byte result vector.

**`is_neighbor` is a linear scan, and the forward rows are sorted by original neighbor id.** 25,286 of 30,150 rows with two or more neighbors are not sorted by the stored dense index, so a binary search has to compare `v_ids[v_adj[k]]`. That search is correct on the current layout. Per query, on this graph:

| degree | linear | binary |
|---:|---:|---:|
| 4 | 1.6 ns | 1.9 ns |
| 8 | 2.5 ns | 2.4 ns |
| 16 | 3.6 ns | 2.9 ns |
| 32 | 6.1 ns | 3.1 ns |
| 64 | 13.8 ns | 3.6 ns |
| 7,085 | 1,288 ns | 37 ns |

The public `is_neighbor` on that hub took 695 ns, which is the dictionary lookup plus the linear scan. At degree 9 the API took 14.4 ns and a direct scan, with the id as the dense index, took 1.4 ns. The two dictionary lookups are the whole cost for small neighborhoods. Binary search wins from about degree 8 upward, and by a lot once vertices get large.

**The batch edge-count pass is already the right tool for many subgraphs.** Sixteen subgraphs of 200 U and 200 V vertices: one batch sweep 0.49 ms, sixteen bound `edge_count`s 0.62 ms, sixteen unbound counts 2.67 ms.

The changes with the largest measured effect are: build the CSR from the edge list when the graph will only be frozen, stop `induce_frozen` from reserving parent-sized neighbor storage, narrow the CSR indexes to `Int32` when they fit, and number dense ids in sorted order so a gap-free `1:n` graph can drop the identity dictionaries. On the query side, `neighbors_*_in_subgraph` should use the bound mask, and `is_neighbor` should binary search once the degree is past a handful of neighbors.
